extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and early-career stand-up comedians (and performers interested in handling onstage failure)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria about what it means to 'bomb' in stand-up comedy and how performers should respond and be judged — covering definition, causes, recovery strategies, audience awareness, and post-bomb professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of bombing
rubrics_metrics.description: To bomb as a comedian means that your jokes don't go over with the crowd and get no laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically refers to an entire set, though a single comedic bit can fall flat. This is the basic failure condition being discussed — lack of audience laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: whole set vs single bit
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically, when a comic says he or she 'bombed,' they are referring to an entire set. However, it is possible that just a single comedic bit falls flat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators/performers should distinguish between an isolated failed joke and a wholesale failure of a set; isolated bombs are common and 'okay.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Material readiness / polish
rubrics_metrics.description: Bombing can be a matter of having new material that hasn't been polished or worked out yet, or it could just be because the comic has had an off night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One criterion for whether material is likely to succeed is how well it has been tested and refined; unpolished new material has higher risk of bombing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composure / how the performer handles the bomb
rubrics_metrics.description: How he or she deals with the joke or act falling flat defines the professional skill of the performer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgment of a comedian is often based less on the fact of bombing and more on the performer's reaction — calmness, control, timing, and professional behavior onstage and afterward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate recovery tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: If you're on stage with an audience that's gone silent, the best thing to do is not to panic and to breathe through the routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended tactics include moving on to another topic entirely or making light of how badly the joke or set missed. Avoid panicking; controlled breathing and pace help salvage the moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of self-deprecation / laugh-at-yourself ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor must be central in your life and the ability to laugh at oneself is equally important to being a good comedian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being able to acknowledge mistakes and make light of them can defuse silence and reconnect with the audience; resilience and self-directed humor are positive traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience awareness / appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: It's important to know your audience to avoid bombing — e.g., don't walk into a Republican Convention and tell jokes attacking their leader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match material to the audience's expectations and sensibilities; failure to do so is an avoidable cause of bombing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context / stakes matter
rubrics_metrics.description: You're not going to be judged for one show very often — unless you're on a reality show competition like 'Last Comic Standing' or 'America's Got Talent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate bombing differently depending on venue and stakes: a single bad performance at a low-stakes gig is less career-defining than bombing on televised competitions or high-profile events.
